# The River’s Post Office

On rainy mornings, Jonas delivered the mail along Bridge Street, although most days the rain was only a rumor. The town called Bellwether because its clock had once possessed a bell, though the bell itself had been gone for eighty years. Jonas knew every resident by the shape of their umbrellas: blue belonged to the doctor, green to the children, black to Mrs. Vale, who never opened her letters unless someone had died. He pretended not to notice that distinction, because Bellwether’s etiquette was built on pretending not to notice things. He whistled, stamped, and left bright red cards beneath flowerpots.

That morning, the river delivered something first. At eleven, while Jonas was sorting fishing licenses beside the post office, a green bottle struck the stone landing with the polite knock of a late guest. Its cork bore the royal seal of Bellwether, though that seal had belonged to the kingdom before the town existed. Inside was a slip of paper, folded into a tiny wing. The ink ran whenever Jonas held it toward the light. He squeezed the paper over the desk, but the drops climbed upward, settling on the ceiling in a shining sentence. No word would stay still.

By noon, the warning had dried enough to read: THE BELL MUST NOT RING TODAY. IT WILL WAKE THE RIVER. Beneath those words, smaller and shakier, someone had added, Please believe us. Tomorrow is very wet. Jonas checked the date. It was tomorrow. The old clock stood at the end of Mill Lane, its empty belfry open to the swallows. Below it, workers were tightening ropes around the sluice gate, preparing the monthly sound test. Their foreman, broad as a wardrobe, waved when he saw Jonas. Everything, apparently, was perfectly ordinary. Somewhere behind him, the river hammered against the bridge.

At one o’clock, the mill workers gathered beneath the clock. Someone brought coffee. Someone else brought opinions. Jonas delivered three telegrams, repaired a hinge on the bakery door, and tried not to imagine what a woken river might look like. Mrs. Vale stopped him at the corner. You have that bottle, she said. I can smell tomorrow on it. He asked what tomorrow wanted. She looked down Bridge Street, where raindrops were crawling upward the windows like silver fish. It wants us, she said, to choose again. The ordinary morning seemed suddenly precious, a road not yet covered in water.

Jonas hurried toward the mill, but a girl intercepted him on the footbridge. She was perhaps twelve, barefoot despite the cold, wearing a yellow coat too large for her. A name was stitched inside the collar: LIO, it said, although Jonas had never seen her. She held out the green bottle. That one’s mine, she told him. I have to return it before noon, or the river will forget my house. He asked where her house was. She pointed downstream, toward a neighborhood on no map, then placed her hand over his heart. You’re late, she whispered. Yesterday is watching.

The mill bell was a replacement, imported from a foundry in the north and mounted only that morning. The foreman assured Jonas that the test would be brief. A measured note, he said, tells us whether the new gate is seated properly. He lifted the rope. Lio seized Jonas’s sleeve. Don’t listen with your ears, she said. Listen with your knees. Confused, he leaned against the stone wall. He felt the vibration before the sound: a deep rhythmic tug, like hundreds of tiny doors being opened underwater. The rope descended. The foreman pulled. Above them, the bell began to rise.

The note landed at 12:01. Its voice was not loud, exactly. It was everywhere: in the teacups, in the paving stones, behind everyone’s eyes. The river answered. A long silver wave lifted the footbridge, slid beneath the post office, and continued into the gardens. Fruit dropped from trees in slow motion. The mill gate groaned as branches pressed against it from below. Lio climbed onto the clock’s pedestal, retrieved the warning from Jonas’s pocket, and shouted over the ringing, Too late! We have to change what we heard! But the workers, dazed and dripping, only stared at each other helplessly.

Then Lio struck the clock face with the empty bottle. Glass cracked. The note vanished. The bell fell silent, and the river froze halfway up the town square. For one breath, nothing moved. Then Jonas ran. He knew the river’s habits now: it had carried a flood through this street six generations ago, taken his parents’ shop, buried the old cinema beneath a week of silt. He had told himself the story was only a story. He sprinted toward the mill, coat flapping, while Lio followed behind, leaving small bright footprints in the mud. Water was already starting to thaw.

At the sluice, the foreman struggled with a winch buried under fallen masonry. The gate would open, and the frozen surge would finish what the bell had begun. Jonas pulled off his coat and climbed onto the wheel. Each step was a world; each breath felt like a small flood. Lio passed him the post office bag. Use your letters, she said. They’re good at holding things together. He laughed, slipped, and caught himself. Below, the river groaned awake. He dropped the bag, trapped the handle beneath a broken spoke, and the wheel held. They turned it backward. The gate fell with a thunderous click.

By evening, Bellwether was damp but dry. The river sank into its bed, carrying leaves, swallows, and one green bottle. Jonas found the note inside, now written in a firm, delighted hand: Thank you. You gave us a better tomorrow. He borrowed a pen. Dear future, he wrote, Thank you for the warning. Your river is beautiful. Visit us soon. He addressed the bottle to Lio’s Neighborhood on No Map and pushed it slowly into the current. That night, no mail arrived. Still, beneath the bridge, a cork clicked against glass, and the river began sorting bright envelopes for morning.
